To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

AGE accumulation in ECM proteins may affect vascular endothelium behaviours such as invasion and proliferation, and that the structural alterations in ECM proteins through glycation-induced crosslink formation may affect the interaction between ECM and vascular endothelial cell, resulting in the attenuation of an adequate neoveselization in diabetic patients.
AGE accumulation in the extracellular matrix may affect endothelial cell behaviours and may contribute to the impairment of angiogenesis in diabetes.
glycated collagen matrix is less susceptible to proteolytic attack by endothelial cells, and that the endothelial cell invasion is inhibited in glycated matrix.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of advanced glycation endproducts (AGE) in the pathogenesis of diabetic complications.
the effect of AGE on the angiogenic activity of endothelial cells in a three-dimensional matrix.
the effects of glycation-induced collagen matrix alterations on the angiogenic behaviour of endothelial cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
glycated collagen is less susceptible to degradation by matrix metalloproteinases and other proteinases.
the glycated collagen lattiices are less prone to be invaded by endothelial cells and that this effect is not due to a decreased plasminogen activity or a decreased MMP-2 and -9 activity.
AGE accumulation in extracellular collagen matrix proteins has been shown to induce matrix protein cross-linking and to reduce the susceptibility of matrix proteolysis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
glycated collagen is not suitable for endothelial cell invasion and cord formation.

AGE cross-linking of collagen may impair the angiogenesis by inhibiting the invasion and cord formation of endothelial cells, and may promote the proliferation of endothelial cells on AGE cross-linked matrix.
the glycation of collagen type I, the major structural component of extracellular matrix (ECM), results in the inhibition of angiogenesis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
AGEs are not only a marker for diabetes but they also contribute to the development and progression of diabetes and its associated complications.
AGEs inhibit angiogenesis by altering the mechanical properties of the collagen matrix.
AGE crosslinking of extracellular matrix (collagen) proteins can inhibit the invasion and tube formation of endothelial cells.
